headline: Six Researchers Win Infosys Prize 2026, Including Legal Scholar Gautam Bhatia
subheadline: Karthik Sastry, Swarun Kumar, Gautam Bhatia, Isha Jain, Riddhipratim Basu and Manoj Kumar Joshi each receive a gold medal, citation and $100,000.
body:
• Six researchers won the Infosys Prize 2026, announced November 12 in Bengaluru by the Infosys Science Foundation — Karthik Sastry, Swarun Kumar, Gautam Bhatia, Isha Jain, Riddhipratim Basu and Manoj Kumar Joshi.
  • Legal scholar Gautam Bhatia won in Humanities and Social Sciences for contributions to constitutional law and legal scholarship.
  • Each laureate receives a gold medal, a citation and a prize purse of $100,000.
  • Since 2024 the prize has focused on researchers under 40; this year the foundation received 222 applications.

The Infosys Science Foundation announced six winners of the Infosys Prize 2026 on November 12 at a press conference in Bengaluru, with legal scholar Gautam Bhatia among the laureates. The prize, established in 2009, is one of India's largest awards for excellence in science and research.

The six laureates are Karthik Sastry in Economics, Swarun Kumar in Engineering and Computer Science, Gautam Bhatia in Humanities and Social Sciences, Isha Jain in Life Sciences, Riddhipratim Basu in Mathematical Sciences and Manoj Kumar Joshi in Physical Sciences, the foundation said. The full winners list was reported by Careers360 and The Hindu BusinessLine.

The six winners and their work

Economics — Karthik Sastry, Princeton University. Recognised for research on climate change, technological innovation and business cycle fluctuations.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeeOe3qiceH/

Engineering and Computer Science — Swarun Kumar, Carnegie Mellon University. Recognised for advances in low-power wireless networks, sensing and control, extending wireless networks beyond data delivery into sensing and interaction with the physical environment.

Humanities and Social Sciences — Gautam Bhatia, Jindal Global Law School and the University of New South Wales. Recognised for contributions to legal scholarship. Research Matters described his prolific scholarship as bridging law with sociology, political theory and moral philosophy, including five influential books focused on using law to build a fair, equal and humane society.

Life Sciences — Isha Jain, Gladstone Institutes and University of California, San Francisco. Recognised for pioneering discoveries in oxygen biology and new therapeutic strategies. Her work has shown that excess oxygen, rather than energy failure, can cause tissue damage in certain mitochondrial diseases.

Mathematical Sciences — Riddhipratim Basu, International Centre for Theoretical Sciences, TIFR, Bengaluru. Recognised for contributions to probability theory and statistical physics, including work on the longstanding slow-bond problem.

Physical Sciences — Manoj Kumar Joshi, Singapore University of Technology and Design. Recognised for experimental advances in quantum simulation using trapped ions and for work on programmable quantum systems.

"This year's laureates are among the world's promising researchers. But remember that this is not a lifetime achievement award. This honour is meant to spur you on to bigger work and to bigger honours."

— Narayana Murthy, Trustee, Infosys Science Foundation

What the prize carries

Each category prize comprises a gold medal, a citation and a prize purse of $100,000 or its equivalent in rupees, the foundation said. The laureates were selected by an international panel of jurors.

From 2024, the prize has shifted focus to honour researchers under the age of 40, emphasising early recognition of exceptional talent. This year the foundation received 222 applications, with the highest number in Engineering and Computer Science, according to Research Matters.

Srinath Batni, President of the Board of Trustees of the Infosys Science Foundation, said in the announcement that recognising exceptional researchers early in their careers gives them encouragement to pursue bold questions and challenge established thinking. The winners were announced by trustees including Batni, K. Dinesh, Kris Gopalakrishnan, Pratima Murthy and S. D. Shibulal, the BusinessLine reported.

For Indian-origin researchers working at universities in the United States, Australia and Singapore — three of this year's six laureates are based outside India — the list is a concise snapshot of where early-career Indian-origin scholarship is being recognised this year, across fields from constitutional law to quantum simulation.

key_takeaways: Six researchers awarded the Infosys Prize 2026 on November 12.
Gautam Bhatia recognized for contributions to constitutional law.
Each laureate receives a gold medal and $100,000 prize.
Prize focuses on researchers under 40 since 2024.
